would like to see a lot more of nature based solutions. And I think that I'm very curious about the value of, the overall value of the Delta or all Deltas. They are these incredibly rich areas ecologically that gather riches from throughout the watershed. Including, and then also tidally. So the biggest bang for the buck of these things, ecologically- is ecological, and not economic. And that, like, I'm very curious to see about an overall shift away from the economics being the prime management tool of the Delta, to more ecosystemic management. And I don't know if you're familiar with the concept of Buffalo Commons? Folks had this idea in the Midwest of in the Great Plains states, just taking a lot of farm land out of production, and restoring it with tall grass prairie and things like that, and restoring buffalo and trying to build up an economy around that. Very interesting concept is, is, it's decades old, but still use the term Buffalo Commons quite a bit. And what would that actually be like in the Delta? We have, we've had some areas where we've considered kind of national sacrifice areas, because there, there's such rich mineral wealth or something, you know, damming rivers, like yeah, it's, it can be it's got huge impacts. But the upside is so great and we're going to go ahead and live with those impacts. And I'm wondering if there's a way we can flip that around, and have a national restoration area, to really use the next century going forward, to really restore those ecosystem functions of the Delta. And how do we do that while still making people whole? You know, kicking people off their properties, you know, even if it's at fair market price, changing lifestyles, moving communities around and things like that, extraordinarily painful and I don't want to be the guy knocking on the door giving people their eviction notices. But what would that look like? What could it look like? I'm not a big believer in you know, everybody, if we do this, everybody will get better. Believe it. Regardless of whatever decision we make, somebody's going to get screwed. And they're going to feel like that's a bad decision. But what are some ways that we can actually really progress towards looking at the Delta primarily as a restoration possibility?

You and I have talked about it, what if we made some of these islands not islands anymore?  We connected them to the adjacent lands that they were once connected to. So we actually get back to actually these are those of the river, and these are the intertidal channels that kind of go between these blocks of land. But how would that change the influence of the salinity in the Delta where the salt water goes? How extensive and impactful that salt water is, because it's really a short time period that it's been as screwed up as it is. Right? We come in and we cut these channels for barges and boats to move through so that we can export stuff. But well how is that influenced the salt water problems vs the rivers themselves and the slews that were there  it's very different, right? Fundamentally, right?

What I’m saying is we’ve got these remnant patches of land that are there what if we reconnect those lands to one another, so that  least the rivers themselves are moving in the directions that they should be. So, It's a little bit different, but similar right?

BM: So by that- is that more the ones that are sort of closer to being at tidal elevation? 

DH:  No, not necessarily. I look at Bradford and Web as an example that does that slew that runs north, south between them. Well what if we, put a barrier between that at the north end and the south end of the slew and then opened up so that those islands are now connected as one you know. More of those kind of closing the gaps…

BM: Ah! So taking the puzzles pieces and making them into one big puzzle piece.

DH: Exactly.  The imagery that I that have gone back to look at to create things like the paleo slews and things like that. To me I can see where those have gone across these different lands and the soils in the imagery piecing all these different things together, I see that. Well, what if they were connected again like would how would that change things? I don’t know the question beyond that other than like, well how does that influence the salinity in this case?  That would be interesting to look.

Connectivity of the channels, you know, The Delta channels are all very, very connected right now. And this may get more at food production and ecosystem benefits without really looking that much at salinity. But you know all these cross connections across the Delta. You know they're great for boats, and the recreation community will kill me if they hear me say it. But what if we cut off some of the cross connections so that there are  dead end slews here and there. You know that we get a little bit more production in those areas for species. Would that be helpful without, you know, changing salinity patterns? I don't know.

 and you close down the the width of the channel there, that means less water is going to come through on the tide. Now, that's a very uneducated engineering view. But you know could you do things like that,

and modifying little bits of infrastructure here and there. But we, we somehow think that that, that map of the Delta with the islands where they are, even though they're all riprapped, is somehow God-given and immutable, you know. Maybe we want to look at changing the geometry of the Delta for hydrodynamic and ecological reasons

I wonder what would happen if you reconfigured the sloughs and tidal reaches in, in the Delta, and Suisun, to resemble the hydrology that would include a lot more dead ends. So, if you remove all these connect, you know. See what happens to the, to the hydraulics and the hydrology of the system if you, if you were to eliminate all these dredged connections that we made in order to move people and stuff around the Delta. So in my, I talked about homogenization earlier.

So go back to a more foundational dendritic hydrology, or, or bathymetry. Bathymetry is more appropriate, I think. So a more, more natural, bathymetry without all these connections and stuff. And I think what you'd find is that you would, you would generate pockets of diversity of habitat, aquatic habitat, in the Delta that don't exist now, because it all mixes in. And that's kind of by design. That's what we wanted. We wanted, we wanted to mix all that stuff in so that we could get it effectively to the pumps and move it south. Well, ecologically, maybe that was the wrong thing to do. It'd be nice to explore that.

Open water places are distinctly different from dead end channels that have title action on them. They're, they're, they're in many ways, they're kind of the antecedent of that. But you, but yeah, yeah, yeah. More open water to me, I mean, I think we should explore that. I think we should explore what more open water looks like, sure. But I don't think-
 
BM: Doesn’t that create less open water, cause you'd be cutting off, I mean, what I was thinking is, if you have, and here's a tract. Here's a tract. Here's a tract. If you just seal them all off, you've just lost all that other channel, so you don't have as much. You just have the now the channel that's around it cause you've changed them together.
 
SC: Oh, yeah, yeah. I guess, yeah. Interesting. Anyway, I think. Yes, I think exploring different bathymetries is worthwhile. I don't think we need to worry about today what, what scenarios. But I mean the bathymetry drives water movement to a very, very large degree. So, playing around with plugs or flood plane connections - that have, those have very significant responses of the hydrology. And I don't think we've done nearly enough to, to convince ourselves of that. As a, as a geomorphologist, I think, I mean, that's what I studied. It was, it was, those landscape, the landscapes that you find are there because of the channel geomorphology. And when you change that, you change what's there. So if you want more of something else, you need to change the hydro, the bathymetry. Anyway.

Definitely, we can do stuff like, you know, yesterday we had a proposal go into the Delta Conservancy, and they approve funding and our project for growing more rice in the Delta. . I said before our project that we're trying to push through or are pushing through with creating more money incentives to get farmers to convert over to wetland farming.
